extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary theory, and writers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and terminology for analyzing narrative discourse (the textual statement) with attention to its relations to story (events) and narrating (the act of telling). Uses Proust as a demanding test case for general narratological categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three distinct notions of "narrative" (story, narrative, narrating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette distinguishes three meanings of 'narrative': (1) the narrative statement or discourse (the text that tells events), (2) the succession of events that are the subject of the discourse (story), and (3) the act of narrating itself (the event of telling). He proposes to use the terms 'story' for the signified/content, 'narrative' for the signifier/discourse/text, and 'narrating' for the producing action/situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating these levels; analytic clarity requires univocal terms. Although the book focuses on narrative (discourse), analysis will necessarily address relations to story and to the narrating act. This terminological distinction is foundational for the whole method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat narrative discourse as the primary object of textual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative (in Genette's chosen limited sense) — the narrative discourse or text — is the aspect directly available to textual analysis and thus is the primary object of study in literary narratology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While story and narrating can be studied via external documents (historical sources, authorial documents), literary analysis should center on the narrative text itself and infer relationships to story and narrating from that text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mood (focalization) and voice (narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette argues that traditional notions of point of view fail to separate two distinct questions: 'who is the character whose point of view orients the narrative perspective?' (mood/focalization) and 'who is the narrator?' (voice). The same point of view can be retained whether the narrative is in first person or third person; conversely, in first-person narratives, the point of view can vary depending on whether events are focalized through the narrator's present consciousness or past consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on the difference between narration and focalization when analyzing 'point of view'; classify narrative phenomena in terms of mood (focalization) vs voice (narratorial level/type) rather than collapsing them into a single 'point of view' label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization: internal vs external
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette's notion of focalization distinguishes internal focalization (narrative focused through a character's consciousness) from what he terms external focalization (narrative focused on a character without access to their thoughts or perceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize debates and refinements: critics (e.g., Mieke Bal) argue that 'external focalization' is a substantially different phenomenon and that treating it as a variant of focalization weakens the concept. Be open to emendations that preserve conceptual precision; use examples (e.g., Hemingway's 'The Killers') to test classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relations between story-time and narrative-time: order, duration, frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette classifies the relations between the time of the story and the time of the narrative under three headings: order (events occur in one order but are narrated in another — e.g., flashback, foreshadowing, in medias res), duration/pace (the narrative devotes differing amounts of textual space to moments — e.g., scene vs summary), and frequency (how often events are recounted relative to how often they occurred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three dimensions systematically when analyzing temporal organization. Note that order and duration are familiar categories, while frequency has been under-discussed and proves crucial for understanding repetition and certain modern techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative and pseudo-iterative modes (frequency specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The iterative mode is when the narrative tells once that something happened frequently; the pseudo-iterative is when the story narrates as though an event happened repeatedly even though its particularity makes it singular (a narrational phrasing that creates an impression of repetition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequency and its figures (iterative/pseudo-iterative) as central devices — they produce distinctive narrative effects (e.g., Proustian repetitions) and have important functions in avant-garde and other narrative strategies. Identify instances and consider their effects on meaning and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of narrative enunciation (the act of narrating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette emphasizes the neglected problem of narrating: the act of producing the narrative discourse itself (who is recounting, and in what situation). The narrating act matters for the existence and the status (fictive or factual) of both the discourse and the recounted events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include analysis of enunciation: determine whether the narrator is actual (authorial) or fictional (character), whether the act of telling bears on truth/falsity of events, and how enunciative positions shape the discourse. Historical and philosophical precedents (e.g., Plato) demonstrate the importance of this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological stance: specific textual study to derive/ test general categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette adopts a dual approach: he develops general narratological concepts through rigorous study of a particular complex work (Proust's Recherche), neither treating the novel merely as illustration nor subordinating theory fully to criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demanding texts (complex or anomalous cases) to test and refine categories — anomalies should prompt conceptual modification. Analysts should move from the particular (text) to the general (categories), while remaining sensitive to the text's irreducible specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat anomalies and marginal phenomena as analytically revealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette argues that features which appear anomalous or marginal (Proustian transgressions of standard categories) are crucial for the system: these exceptions often determine or reveal the norms and prompt necessary refinements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering narrative 'violations' of a category, analyze them carefully rather than dismissing them; use such anomalies to test the adequacy of the taxonomy and to inspire emendations to the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a systematic technical vocabulary for narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Genette notes that common terms like 'point of view', 'flashback', 'omniscient narrator', etc., have been developed ad hoc and lack a comprehensive systematic survey; his work aims to identify, name, and illustrate the basic constituents and techniques of narrative (e.g., Order, Duration, Frequency, Mood, Voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and apply a consistent, systematic terminology when describing narrative techniques; map observed phenomena to the taxonomy (order, duration, frequency, mood, voice) to increase analytical precision and comparability across texts.
